title: Driving Namibia as a Group? How a Self Drive Convoy Keeps Everyone Together
meta_title: Namibia Self Drive Convoy: Routes, Radios and Rules
meta_description: How a Namibia self drive convoy works for groups: vehicles, drivers, an 11-day route with distances, road rules, park fees and when a lead guide pays off.
excerpt: A Namibia self drive convoy lets a group drive its own 4x4s on one route. Here is how to split vehicles, plan the loop, stay together on gravel and decide on a guide.
content:
A Namibia self drive convoy is a group of two or more rented 4x4s driving the same route together, usually from Windhoek to Sossusvlei, Swakopmund, Damaraland and Etosha, with lodges booked in advance and, if you choose, a guide in a lead vehicle. Each household drives itself, but nobody is ever alone on a remote gravel road.

Friends, extended families and clubs often love the idea of driving Namibia together, then hit the hard questions: how many cars, who leads, how to keep everyone in sight on dusty roads, and whether a guide is worth paying for. This guide answers those questions from our Nairobi planning desk, and our page on how we organise a group safari explains deposits, rooming lists and timelines. If you prefer a fully guided trip, browse our Namibia safari packages instead.

Quick Facts

  • Typical length: 10 to 12 days for the classic Windhoek, Sossusvlei, Swakopmund, Damaraland and Etosha loop
  • Group size: 3 to 6 vehicles per convoy works best; larger groups split into two convoys
  • Roads: Mostly gravel outside the main tar routes; drive on the left
  • Speed limits: 120 km/h on tar and 100 km/h on gravel by law, though 80 km/h is safer on gravel
  • Park fees: N$280 per international adult per day at Etosha and Namib-Naukluft from 1 April 2026, plus a small vehicle fee (checked November 2026)
  • Best months: May to October for cooler days and Etosha waterhole viewing
  • Golden rule: No driving after dark: plan every day to arrive before sunset

What Is a Namibia Self Drive Convoy?

A Namibia self drive convoy is a shared road trip in which each couple, family or pair of friends drives their own 4x4 on a common itinerary, staying at the same lodges or campsites each night. The group shares the route, the bookings and the support, while every vehicle keeps its own pace and privacy during the day.

The format suits Namibia unusually well. Distances are long, traffic is light and the main gravel roads are graded and signposted, so confident drivers do not need a guide to find the way. What they do need is a plan that keeps the group together, and someone thinking about fuel, punctures and arrival times so the holiday does not turn into a logistics exercise.

Guided convoy with a lead vehicle

In a guided convoy, a professional guide drives the front vehicle, carries a radio for every car, and briefs the group each morning on the day's distance, fuel stops and road conditions. The guide also explains the landscapes and wildlife at stops, deals with lodges and helps change tyres. This is the version we recommend for first-time African drivers and for groups with children.

Independent Namibia self drive convoy

An independent Namibia self drive convoy has no guide. The group follows a pre-booked itinerary with route notes, meets at agreed points, and relies on each other and the rental company's roadside assistance if something goes wrong. It costs less and feels freer, but someone in the group has to take the leader's role every day, and that person rarely gets a holiday.

Is a Convoy Better Than One Big Guided Vehicle for a Group?

A convoy is better for groups that want independence, mixed pace and privacy between households, while one large guided vehicle is better for groups that want to relax, learn and avoid driving altogether. A Namibia self drive convoy gives each car its own schedule within the day; a guided vehicle gives everyone a driver and full-time commentary.

The honest trade-off is energy. On a Namibia self drive convoy, driving gravel for five or six hours, several days in a row, is tiring, and the driver misses much of the view. Our comparison of guided Namibia safaris and self-drive goes deeper on that question for couples. For groups, the table below is a fair summary.

OptionBest forTrade-off
Guided Namibia self drive convoyFamilies, first-time 4x4 drivers, groups of 3 to 6 carsHigher cost than going alone, but a guide handles problems and briefings
Independent convoyExperienced drivers, clubs, friends who have driven gravel beforeCheapest; one group member effectively becomes the trip leader
One guided group vehicleGroups who want no driving, photographers, older travellersLess flexibility and privacy; everyone moves together all day
Split group (some drive, some ride)Mixed groups where only some want to driveNeeds a guide vehicle with spare seats for non-drivers

Which Route Works for a Group, and How Many Days?

The route that works best for a first Namibia self drive convoy is the classic loop: Windhoek to Sossusvlei, then Swakopmund on the coast, Damaraland in the north-west, Etosha National Park and back to Windhoek. It covers dunes, ocean, desert-adapted wildlife and Etosha's waterholes in 10 to 12 days, with two nights in most places.

Groups move more slowly than a single car. Fuel stops take longer when five vehicles queue at one pump, toilet breaks multiply, and photo stops happen more often. As a rule, add 30 to 60 minutes to any published driving time when you plan a Namibia self drive convoy. The distances below come from a published Namibia distance chart and are approximate.

LegDistanceApproximate drive time
Windhoek to Sesriem (Sossusvlei gate)About 320 kmAbout 5 hours
Sesriem to SwakopmundAbout 300 kmAbout 6 hours on gravel
Windhoek to Swakopmund (direct)About 360 kmAbout 4 hours on tar
Swakopmund to Okaukuejo (Etosha)About 570 kmAbout 6 hours; better split with a Damaraland stop
Twyfelfontein to OkaukuejoAbout 360 kmAbout 3 hours
Okaukuejo to WindhoekAbout 440 kmAbout 5 hours, mostly tar

A sample 11-day Namibia self drive convoy loop

  • Day 1: Arrive at Hosea Kutako International Airport, collect vehicles, vehicle briefing, night in Windhoek
  • Days 2-3: Drive to the Sossusvlei area; dawn at the dunes and Deadvlei on day 3
  • Days 4-5: Drive to Swakopmund via the Kuiseb and Gaub passes; a free day on the coast
  • Days 6-7: Drive to Damaraland via Spitzkoppe; rock engravings at Twyfelfontein
  • Days 8-10: Etosha National Park, ideally one night in the west and two in the east
  • Day 11: Drive back to Windhoek and return vehicles before your flight

Our 5 Days Namibia Adventure covers the Sossusvlei and Swakopmund half of this loop, and the 6-day Namibian Culture and Scenery Tour covers Damaraland and Kaokoland, so a group can see how each section runs before deciding which parts to drive. For more on the park itself, read our guide to planning an Etosha safari around the waterholes.

How Should a Group Split Into Vehicles, Drivers and Rooms?

A group should split into vehicles of two to four people, with at least two confident drivers in every car, so that nobody drives every hour of every day. On a Namibia self drive convoy, households normally share a vehicle, and the most experienced gravel driver sits in the last car, not the first, to help anyone who stops.

Choosing the 4x4 for a Namibia self drive convoy

Most groups rent double-cab 4x4 pick-ups or SUVs with high clearance. A double cab takes two to four adults with luggage in the canopy. For a lodge-based Namibia self drive convoy you do not need rooftop tents; for a camping trip, check that each vehicle comes with a fridge, two spare wheels, a compressor and full camping kit. Ask the rental company to supply identical or similar vehicles, so drivers can help each other with jacks and tools.

Every driver must be named on the rental agreement and insurance. Rental companies set their own minimum ages and excess levels, so check those terms before you assign drivers, and make sure the group's travel insurance also covers self-driving.

Rooming and lodge sizes

Many desert and Damaraland lodges have only a few dozen beds, so a Namibia self drive convoy of 12 to 20 people often takes most of a lodge. Book 9 to 12 months ahead for the dry season, and send a final rooming list with each guest's name, room type and dietary needs. If one lodge cannot hold everyone, split the group between two nearby lodges and keep the same meeting point for the next morning.

Driving Rules and Convoy Discipline on Namibian Roads

Namibia's main rules are: drive on the left, wear seat belts, keep to 120 km/h on tar and 100 km/h on gravel, and never drive after dark. On a Namibia self drive convoy, add three group rules: keep well back from the dust ahead, stay in radio contact, and never leave the last vehicle on its own.

The Namibian embassy driving guidance confirms that you need a full licence valid in your home country, plus an international permit if it is not in English, and that seat belts are compulsory in hire cars. In practice, 80 km/h is a sensible top speed on gravel, because loose stones and corrugations make braking and steering unpredictable at higher speeds.

  • Dust spacing: drop back until the dust from the car ahead has cleared; on busy gravel that can mean several hundred metres
  • Radios: one two-way radio per car, with a check-in every time the convoy turns or stops
  • Meeting points: agree fixed regroup points such as fuel stations, pass summits and park gates
  • Fuel: fill up at every station you pass; stations are far apart in the south and north-west
  • Punctures: stop the whole convoy; everyone waits until the spare is fitted and checked
  • Night driving: plan arrivals by mid-afternoon, because wildlife and livestock wander onto unfenced roads after dark

Inside Etosha National Park

Etosha has its own rules: stay inside your vehicle except at rest camps and fenced rest areas, keep to marked roads, observe the 60 km/h speed limit and be through the gates before they close at sunset. Each Namibia self drive convoy should spread out inside the park, as five cars arriving together at one waterhole crowd other visitors and disturb animals. Pick two or three waterholes each morning and rotate between them.

When Is the Best Time for a Group Road Trip in Namibia?

The best time for a Namibia self drive convoy is May to October, the dry season, when days are cooler, skies are clear and Etosha's wildlife gathers at waterholes. July and August are the busiest months, so groups need early bookings. November to April brings heat and rain, mainly in the north and centre.

Desert heat matters more for a convoy than for a single car, because a group spends more time outside at fuel stops and viewpoints. December and January bring midday temperatures that make long gravel days hard work, although Etosha turns green and quiet. Our month-by-month guide to the best time to visit Namibia has the detail, and our list of first-time Namibia safari mistakes covers the planning errors we see most often.

What Does a Group Self-Drive Trip in Namibia Cost?

A Namibia self drive convoy costs less per person than a fully guided private trip, because each household pays for its own vehicle and fuel rather than a guide and driver for the whole group. The final figure depends mainly on vehicle hire, lodge level, whether you add a guide, and the season.

Park fees are the one fixed cost we can quote. From 1 April 2026, international adults pay N$280 per day at Etosha and Namib-Naukluft, plus a small per-vehicle charge (checked November 2026; confirm before you book). Everything else varies by supplier and date, so the table shows what drives each cost rather than invented figures.

Cost itemWho paysWhat changes the price
4x4 hire and insurancePer vehicle, shared by its passengersVehicle type, season, excess level, one-way or return
FuelPer vehicleTotal distance (roughly 2,000 km or more on the classic loop) and engine size
Lodges or campsitesPer personLodge level, room type, peak dry-season dates
Park feesPer person per day, plus per vehicleNumber of days in Etosha and Namib-Naukluft
Lead guide and vehicleShared by the whole groupTrip length; cheaper per person as the group grows
Radios and extra kitPer vehicleUsually a small daily rental

The guide's cost is the line that changes most with group size. Shared across five or six cars on a Namibia self drive convoy, a lead guide adds a modest amount per person; for two cars it is a much bigger share. Insider Tips

  • Brief together: Hold one vehicle handover for the whole Namibia self drive convoy so everyone learns the same jack, tyre and 4x4 settings
  • Swap leaders: On an independent convoy, rotate the lead car daily so one person does not carry the whole trip
  • Shared group chat: Mobile signal disappears for hours, so agree the day's plan at breakfast, not on the road
  • Cash for fuel: Carry some Namibian dollars in each car in case a station card machine is down
  • Early starts: Leave by 7am on long days so the whole convoy arrives with daylight to spare
  • Visa and passports: UK, US and many EU visitors need a visa on arrival; passports must be valid for at least 6 months

Before any Namibia self drive convoy leaves Windhoek, check entry rules. They changed in April 2025, when Namibia began charging visa fees to visitors from many countries that were previously exempt. The Namibian embassy visa notice lists eligible nationalities and documents; recent official notices give the fee as N$1,600, but confirm it before you fly (checked November 2026). Frequently Asked Questions

Do I need a guide for a Namibia self drive convoy?

A guide is not required for a Namibia self drive convoy, because the main gravel routes are well signed. Groups with first-time 4x4 drivers, children or more than four vehicles usually add a lead guide, who sets the pace, handles punctures and radios ahead to lodges, so nobody is left solving problems alone.

How many vehicles can travel in one convoy?

Most groups find three to six vehicles the practical size for a Namibia self drive convoy. Beyond six, dust spacing stretches the line over several kilometres, fuel stops take far longer and small desert lodges struggle to room everyone. Larger groups usually split into two convoys a day apart on the same route.

What driving licence do I need to drive in Namibia?

Visitors need a full driving licence valid in their country of residence, and an International Driving Permit if that licence is not in English, according to Namibian embassy guidance. Some rental companies ask every driver for an International Driving Permit anyway, so it is simplest to get one before you travel. Namibia drives on the left.

Is driving in Namibia safe for a group?

A Namibia self drive convoy is generally safe for a group that respects gravel-road speeds, never drives after dark and keeps vehicles in radio contact. Most serious incidents involve rollovers from going too fast on loose gravel, not crime or wildlife. A convoy adds safety, because a second vehicle is always nearby to help after a puncture or breakdown.

How many days does a Namibia self drive convoy need?

A Namibia self drive convoy covering Sossusvlei, Swakopmund, Damaraland and Etosha needs 10 to 12 days. Shorter trips are possible, but group convoys move more slowly than a single car, and long transfer days of 400 to 570 km leave little time to enjoy each stop. Twelve days allows two nights in most places.

Final Thoughts

A Namibia self drive convoy gives a group the freedom of a road trip with the safety of company: three to six 4x4s, a fixed route, lodges booked well ahead and firm rules on dust, radios and daylight. For first-time gravel drivers, a lead guide turns a demanding drive into an easy one.
